deepDive.title: Coriolis effect — why cyclones spin (and why they spin opposite in two hemispheres)
deepDive.body: In Class 7 you saw cyclones spin. Class 9 reveals WHY — Earth is rotating beneath the moving air. The CORIOLIS EFFECT: any object moving over a rotating planet appears (to an observer on the surface) to curve. In the Northern Hemisphere, moving objects deflect RIGHT; in the Southern, LEFT. So Bay of Bengal cyclones rotate ANTICLOCKWISE; cyclones near Australia rotate CLOCKWISE. The effect is zero at the equator and strongest at the poles — that's why cyclones never form within ~5° of the equator (no Coriolis to start the spin). Indian Ocean cyclones always form north of ~10°N or south of ~10°S. Sub-tropical Indian states (Tamil Nadu, Odisha, West Bengal) are in the cyclone zone.
deepDive.nextStepHint: Class 11 derives Coriolis force quantitatively: F = -2mΩ × v.

deepDive.title: Cyclone genesis — why warm ocean water is the fuel
deepDive.body: In Class 7 you saw cyclones form over warm seas. Class 11 details the mechanism. CYCLONE GENESIS requires: (1) sea surface temperature ≥ 26.5°C through 50+ m depth — provides moisture and energy. (2) Low vertical wind shear — winds blowing the same direction at different altitudes (no shear = vertical column intact). (3) Pre-existing low-pressure disturbance (e.g., monsoon trough). (4) At least ~5° from equator (Coriolis spin). (5) Moist mid-troposphere (no dry air to disrupt convection). The Bay of Bengal has all five most years — that's why ~80% of Indian cyclones form there, not in the Arabian Sea. Eye wall replacement: as a cyclone matures, the outer rain bands form a new wall, the old wall collapses — the storm 're-organises'. This is what makes intensity hard to forecast.
deepDive.nextStepHint: NEET / IIT-meteorology students study Saffir-Simpson scale and the role of CAPE (convective available potential energy).

deepDive.title: Air pressure with altitude — why aircraft cabins are pressurised
deepDive.body: Class 7 says air pressure is the 'weight of air above'. Class 10 makes it quantitative. At sea level, atmospheric pressure ≈ 1013 hPa (or 1 atm). Every 10 m up, pressure drops by ~1 hPa initially. At Manali (2050 m): ~780 hPa (77% of sea-level). At Mount Everest base camp: ~500 hPa. At 10 km cruising altitude (where aircraft fly): only ~265 hPa — too low to breathe. So airplane cabins are pressurised to ~750 hPa (equivalent to ~2400 m altitude). When a plane suddenly depressurises (rare but happens), oxygen masks deploy automatically. The cabin doors are slightly inward-curved so cabin pressure pushes them shut tighter, never opens them in flight. Air pressure isn't optional engineering — it's life support.
deepDive.nextStepHint: Class 12 introduces gas laws (PV=nRT) — the math behind altitude pressure equations.
